cues.text: Section nine: governance and value realisation.
Let us begin with value realisation.
Value realisation is the process of converting investments into actual business outcomes.

To make this real, you should define several things before the investment is made: the benefits you expect, the baseline you are starting from, the target you want to reach, the accountable owner, the measurement method, and the review date.
Having all of these in place beforehand means that success can later be judged against something concrete.
It is also important to distinguish an output from an outcome.
A deployed platform is an output; it is simply something that has been delivered.
Reduced delivery costs or improved customer retention are outcomes; they are the actual business results the investment was meant to produce.
Next, consider the frameworks and structures that support governance.
COBIT provides governance and management objectives that connect technology investment to enterprise goals.
ITIL supports service delivery, change management, incident management and continual improvement.
In addition, a joint IT-finance portfolio board can evaluate performance, approve the reallocation of funds, and stop projects that no longer justify investment.
Now, how do we know whether value is being realised?
We monitor key performance indicators, or KPIs, in four groups.
First, financial KPIs: budget variance, total cost of ownership, return on investment, and unit cost.
Second, operational KPIs: cycle time, availability, and throughput.
Third, customer KPIs: retention and satisfaction.
Fourth, capability KPIs: skills and adoption.
Dashboards and periodic reviews should be used to adapt allocations as the evidence comes in.
Finally, we must consider financial risk.
The financial risks named here are cost overruns, currency fluctuations, vendor price increases, demand uncertainty, integration failure, and unrealised benefits.
These can be mitigated through scenario analysis, contingencies, staged funding, transparent contracts, architecture portability, risk registers, and benefit tracking.

Notice how several of these mitigations connect back to value realisation itself: staged funding lets you stop or redirect money when results fall short, and benefit tracking keeps attention on whether the promised outcomes actually arrive.
